title: Flattering Lips and Flawless Words
superscription: For the choirmaster. According to Sheminith. A Psalm of David.

verses.text: Help, O LORD, for the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among men.
They lie to one another; they speak with flattering lips and a double heart.
May the LORD cut off all flattering lips and every boastful tongue.
They say, "With our tongues we will prevail. We own our lips—who can be our master?"
"For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise," says the LORD. "I will bring safety to him who yearns."
The words of the LORD are flawless, like silver refined in a furnace, like gold purified sevenfold.
You, O LORD, will keep us; You will forever guard us from this generation.
The wicked wander freely, and vileness is exalted among men.

context.author: The title says “of David” (Hebrew le-David), which can mean by David, for David or about David. Seventy-three psalms carry his name; tradition and the New Testament take many of them as his.
context.genre: Psalm: a song or prayer in Hebrew poetry
context.audience: Israel at worship in Jerusalem, and every reader who prays
context.setting: “Help, O LORD, for the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among men” (v.1). Everyone lies, speaking “with flattering lips and a double heart” (v.2), boasting, “With our tongues we will prevail. We own our lips—who can be our master?” (v.4). Then God Himself speaks: “For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise” (v.5). Against all the lying words stand God’s words: “The words of the LORD are flawless, like silver refined in a furnace, like gold purified sevenfold” (v.6).
context.custom: Silver was refined by melting it in a clay crucible and skimming off the dross, again and again, until it was pure (Proverbs 17:3; Malachi 3:3). Seven was the number of completeness, so “sevenfold” means perfectly pure. A “double heart” (literally “a heart and a heart”) is a divided, two-faced heart.
context.timelineImmediate: Psalm 13 asks four times, “How long, O LORD?”
context.timelineBible: Proverbs says, “Every word of God is flawless; He is a shield to those who take refuge in Him” (Proverbs 30:5). Micah 7:2 laments in the same way that the godly have perished from the land. James warns that the tongue “boasts of great things” (James 3:5).

translation.meaning: Faithful, godly, loyal; related to chesed, steadfast love.
To smelt, refine, test by fire.

gospelParallels.note: Every careless word will be judged.
Faith refined by fire, more precious than gold.

otBackground.note: Every word of God is flawless.
The godly have vanished from the land.
He will sit as a refiner of silver.

overview.summary: In an age of flattering lies, God promises to arise for the oppressed, and His words stand pure like refined silver.
overview.settingLine: A world full of smooth talk.

history.t: Prophets describe whole generations of liars.
The first to suffer from lies.

archaeology.t: Clay crucibles and slag from metalworking are found at Iron Age sites.
Hoards of cut silver used as money are found in Judah and Philistia.

overview.discussion: God’s words are “flawless” (v.6). How do my words compare with His? Where do I flatter or speak with a double heart?
overview.book: The book of Psalms · 150 psalms (1-60 in the app so far). Israel’s songs and prayers: praise, lament, thanks, trust and wisdom, many of them by David.
overview.author: David

historicalImage.caption: Part of the Great Psalms Scroll (11Q5) from Qumran Cave 11, copied in the first half of the first century AD. More copies of the Psalms were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls than of any other book.
